newsitem.title: USA: PSA eyeing GFOA safety tips on hiring dealers, FA.
newsitem.headline: PSA eyeing GFOA safety tips on hiring dealers, FA.

text.p: PSA officials generally declined to comment on Wednesday on draft GFOA safety tips for municipal bond issuers in the process of selecting municipal bond underwriters and financial advisers.

The Government Finance Officers Association's panel on debt and fiscal policy approved the five-page "recommended practice" - designed to help localities head off enforcement problems plaguing the $1.3 trillion muni market for months -, at a meeting here this week.
The proposal could go before GFOA's executive board for approval as early as next month, a GFOA spokesperson said.
A spokesman for Heather Ruth, president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, said Ruth had not yet reviewed GFOA's draft recommendations and, therefore, had no comment.
Micah Green, PSA's executive vice president, said he is reviewing the document, but cannot comment because he is still unsure about how much it differs from current industry practice.

The recommendations come in the wake of last month's sentencing by a federal judge of former Lazard Freres & Co. investment banker Mark Ferber to 33 months in prison and a $1 million fine on 47 counts of fraud and corruption.

The conviction centered on an improperly disclosed contract that Ferber maintained with Merrill Lynch & Co. to advise government clients. Merrill and Lazard in late 1995 paid a total of $24 million in fines to settle the matter with the U.S. Attorney's Office.

The draft procedure urges municipalities to issue detailed requests for proposals (RFPs) before selecting bond professionals, to review existing contracts regularly, and to consider paying advisors on an hourly basis.
To avoid conficts of interest, localities should not make fees contingent on the sale of bonds, the panel recommends.

The panel said RFPs should include a number of questions, including whether there are any "finders fees, fee splitting, or other contractual arrangements of the firm that could present a real or perceived conflict of interest."
RFPs also should ask whether the Securities and Exchange Commission or other regulators are currently investigating firms and whether there are previous enforcement actions.
